newsitem.title: INDIA: Bombay blue chips end mixed in featureless trade.
newsitem.headline: Bombay blue chips end mixed in featureless trade.

text.p: Bombay stocks ended with little change in lacklustre trade on Monday, as postponement by the government of a long pending increase in oil prices restricted fresh buying support, traders said.
A holiday in London and US stock markets also contributed to dull trading volumes, they said.
"Volumes in blue chips were pretty bad," said Ketan Jhaveri, chief dealer at Kotak Securities, the Indian affiliate of Goldman Sachs.
A policy-making body of India's United Front government on Sunday failed to come to a decision to raise oil product prices.
"The hike would have put to rest all speculation about oil prices," Jhaveri said. "Now, the issue has been left hanging."

The government's inability to take a decision on raising prices of oil products has been taken negatively by markets, with analysts saying that the move reflected lack of unity in the ruling United Front.

The widening gap between India's oil demand and domestic supplies called for a 20-25 percent price increase, but political pressures will force the government to restrict the increase for kerosene, analysts said. Kerosene is the basic cooking and lighting fuel for about 300 million poor Indians.
Shares of Indian Petrochemical Corporation Ltd (IPCL) ended 3.50 rupees lower at 124.25 after the firm posted a 15 percent drop in 1996/97 (April-March) net profit.
Lower import tariffs and depressed international prices of chemicals and petrochemicals affected sales realisations, the company said on Monday.
Tata Engineering & Locomotive Company Ltd shares rose 8.50 rupees to 400.0 with over 844,154 shares traded at the Bombay exchange ahead of the firm's 1996/97 results due on Tuesday.
The truck-maker is expected to post an average net profit of 7.20 billion, up from 5.3 billion last year, analysts said.
